text: 1 comment; jeredaw7161d1fa2a says: As you note, the Regulations specifically mention Ukraine. Is it appropriate for the legislation to specifically single out one side in a particular conflict? I think, no. I note that it doesn’t sound as though his sins are any worse than those of many who write in support of Israel regarding the current conflict in Gaza. Searching through the judgment, I see lots of references to propaganda, misinformation and disinformation. With no particulars whatever of anything he might have said that is not true. And no indication of whether the court ever examined whether anything he said is not true. Loading... Reply Leave a Reply You must be logged in to post a comment.
html:
1 comment;

  1. jeredaw7161d1fa2asays:

    As you note, the Regulations specifically mention Ukraine. Is it appropriate for the legislation to specifically single out one side in a particular conflict? I think, no. I note that it doesn’t sound as though his sins are any worse than those of many who write in support of Israel regarding the current conflict in Gaza.

    Searching through the judgment, I see lots of references to propaganda, misinformation and disinformation. With no particulars whatever of anything he might have said that is not true. And no indication of whether the court ever examined whether anything he said is not true.

title: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models
label: wrongful
text: I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math. Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry". I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious. I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range. Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one. Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task. Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems. Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't. I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific. Altitude We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free. Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in. That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambitious. We'll start basic and get a little bit more ambitious with each step: As input, most reviews want to know what changed this quarter, why, and what should be done about it. Resist the urge to just update whatever numbers are in the template - give the model too as much data as you can get your hands on so it can understand your business: "Tell me what changed this quarter, why, and what we should do about it." Meetings (the good kind, anyway) ideally end with some decisions. Ask Claude: "Work out which three decisions are most urgent in the face of everything you've learned, and start working on potential directions with for/against arguments." QBRs are from a time when good reviews required humans to carefully sift through data, figure out what the data means, and if the business should adjust. Ask Claude: "The review exists so leadership catches problems early and moves money and people to the right places. Design a better way to do that than a quarterly deck, show from our own history that it would have caught things sooner, and run it beside the current one for a quarter." The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors. A good tell-tale sign that ambition in altitude is a good idea is if you're going to have meetings to discuss whatever you're working on. There are currently limits ("Claude, go make money" doesn't seem to work for most businesses by itself in 2026), but I generally see that models seem to be able to operate at higher levels of abstraction the more capable they become. Altitude is also where people find durable workflows that take the human out of the loop, making it less necessary for you to constantly update the model with task after task. Doing this well often involves changing your workflow - in order to let Claude make sure our app is crash-free, I first had to make sure it can easily fetch crash reports, understand which app version maps to what git commit, and give it access to Windows, macOS, and Linux computers so it can actually independently reproduce and verify fixes. Depth Sometimes, you just want a task executed really well. Being ambitious in depth means pushing the model to use the tools, techniques, media, and knowledge employed by the best professionals in the field - and to keep pushing until even those people might learn something new from your work. Let's continue with our Acme Inc example of a quarterly business review deck. Assume for a second that Acme Inc struggles with some user churn (customer loss over time). I've found a mix of the following techniques useful: Insist on the same instruments used by the best in the industry: When prompted to act like a professional, models often switch vocabulary without actually switching methods. To work on our problem with depth, we need to use the same tools as the best data scientists and statisticians. When Claude reaches for markdown tables, insist on the use of databases and statistical models. You don't necessarily have to know what the experts use, Claude usually does. Pick unreasonable goals and tell the model that they're very reasonable: You need your website to load in 5s instead of 10s? Ask for 200ms. Does something seem impossible to the model? Reiterate that it's very much solvable, it just needs to keep going. Challenge what you know: Especially in business, a lot of things we believe to be true are rough approximations of reality. Give the model access to the raw information and data and ask it to adversarially check assumptions. "We believe churn is an onboarding problem. Try to reproduce that from the raw data." Produce new knowledge: Easily tacked onto challenging what you know - once Claude is already deep inside the data, ask it to find blind spots. "Build a simulation of our customers that reproduces the last year from our logs. Then find the earliest signal of churn we don't know about yet, and show it predicts on data it has not seen." Use an outside judge: Do not ask the model to judge itself. I assume that this will eventually be solved with increasing model intelligence, but in October 2026, I implore you to insist on outside validation. Ideally that's a tool the model can run to get feedback immediately. A simple prompt that often helps me: I want a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one. Before rewriting it: (1) say what a top professional in this field would do here that I'm not asking for; (2) name the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested for me; (3) name the specific methods and tools they would use; (4) say what, other than you or me, would show the result is right. Then rewrite my prompt to ask for exactly that. Range In short, being ambitious in range means that we consider our work from the perspective of different fields - more fields than would have been economical in the past. This isn't a particularly unique insight, every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents. As AI products make it easier and easier to run mu
html:
I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math.

Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry".

I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious.

I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range.

  • Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one.
  • Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task.
  • Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems.
  • Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't.

I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific.

Altitude

We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free.

Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in.That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambit…[truncated]

title: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models
label: wrongful
text: I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math. Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry". I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious. I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range. Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one. Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task. Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems. Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't. I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific. Altitude We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free. Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in. That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambitious. We'll start basic and get a little bit more ambitious with each step: As input, most reviews want to know what changed this quarter, why, and what should be done about it. Resist the urge to just update whatever numbers are in the template - give the model too as much data as you can get your hands on so it can understand your business: "Tell me what changed this quarter, why, and what we should do about it." Meetings (the good kind, anyway) ideally end with some decisions. Ask Claude: "Work out which three decisions are most urgent in the face of everything you've learned, and start working on potential directions with for/against arguments." QBRs are from a time when good reviews required humans to carefully sift through data, figure out what the data means, and if the business should adjust. Ask Claude: "The review exists so leadership catches problems early and moves money and people to the right places. Design a better way to do that than a quarterly deck, show from our own history that it would have caught things sooner, and run it beside the current one for a quarter." The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors. A good tell-tale sign that ambition in altitude is a good idea is if you're going to have meetings to discuss whatever you're working on. There are currently limits ("Claude, go make money" doesn't seem to work for most businesses by itself in 2026), but I generally see that models seem to be able to operate at higher levels of abstraction the more capable they become. Altitude is also where people find durable workflows that take the human out of the loop, making it less necessary for you to constantly update the model with task after task. Doing this well often involves changing your workflow - in order to let Claude make sure our app is crash-free, I first had to make sure it can easily fetch crash reports, understand which app version maps to what git commit, and give it access to Windows, macOS, and Linux computers so it can actually independently reproduce and verify fixes. Depth Sometimes, you just want a task executed really well. Being ambitious in depth means pushing the model to use the tools, techniques, media, and knowledge employed by the best professionals in the field - and to keep pushing until even those people might learn something new from your work. Let's continue with our Acme Inc example of a quarterly business review deck. Assume for a second that Acme Inc struggles with some user churn (customer loss over time). I've found a mix of the following techniques useful: Insist on the same instruments used by the best in the industry: When prompted to act like a professional, models often switch vocabulary without actually switching methods. To work on our problem with depth, we need to use the same tools as the best data scientists and statisticians. When Claude reaches for markdown tables, insist on the use of databases and statistical models. You don't necessarily have to know what the experts use, Claude usually does. Pick unreasonable goals and tell the model that they're very reasonable: You need your website to load in 5s instead of 10s? Ask for 200ms. Does something seem impossible to the model? Reiterate that it's very much solvable, it just needs to keep going. Challenge what you know: Especially in business, a lot of things we believe to be true are rough approximations of reality. Give the model access to the raw information and data and ask it to adversarially check assumptions. "We believe churn is an onboarding problem. Try to reproduce that from the raw data." Produce new knowledge: Easily tacked onto challenging what you know - once Claude is already deep inside the data, ask it to find blind spots. "Build a simulation of our customers that reproduces the last year from our logs. Then find the earliest signal of churn we don't know about yet, and show it predicts on data it has not seen." Use an outside judge: Do not ask the model to judge itself. I assume that this will eventually be solved with increasing model intelligence, but in October 2026, I implore you to insist on outside validation. Ideally that's a tool the model can run to get feedback immediately. A simple prompt that often helps me: I want a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one. Before rewriting it: (1) say what a top professional in this field would do here that I'm not asking for; (2) name the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested for me; (3) name the specific methods and tools they would use; (4) say what, other than you or me, would show the result is right. Then rewrite my prompt to ask for exactly that. Range In short, being ambitious in range means that we consider our work from the perspective of different fields - more fields than would have been economical in the past. This isn't a particularly unique insight, every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents. As AI products make it easier and easier to run mu

I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math.

Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry".

I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious.

I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range.

  • Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one.
  • Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task.
  • Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems.
  • Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't.

I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific.

Altitude

We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free.

Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in.That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambit…[truncated]

title: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models
label: wrongful
text: I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math. Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry". I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious. I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range. Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one. Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task. Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems. Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't. I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific. Altitude We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free. Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in. That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambitious. We'll start basic and get a little bit more ambitious with each step: As input, most reviews want to know what changed this quarter, why, and what should be done about it. Resist the urge to just update whatever numbers are in the template - give the model too as much data as you can get your hands on so it can understand your business: "Tell me what changed this quarter, why, and what we should do about it." Meetings (the good kind, anyway) ideally end with some decisions. Ask Claude: "Work out which three decisions are most urgent in the face of everything you've learned, and start working on potential directions with for/against arguments." QBRs are from a time when good reviews required humans to carefully sift through data, figure out what the data means, and if the business should adjust. Ask Claude: "The review exists so leadership catches problems early and moves money and people to the right places. Design a better way to do that than a quarterly deck, show from our own history that it would have caught things sooner, and run it beside the current one for a quarter." The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors. A good tell-tale sign that ambition in altitude is a good idea is if you're going to have meetings to discuss whatever you're working on. There are currently limits ("Claude, go make money" doesn't seem to work for most businesses by itself in 2026), but I generally see that models seem to be able to operate at higher levels of abstraction the more capable they become. Altitude is also where people find durable workflows that take the human out of the loop, making it less necessary for you to constantly update the model with task after task. Doing this well often involves changing your workflow - in order to let Claude make sure our app is crash-free, I first had to make sure it can easily fetch crash reports, understand which app version maps to what git commit, and give it access to Windows, macOS, and Linux computers so it can actually independently reproduce and verify fixes. Depth Sometimes, you just want a task executed really well. Being ambitious in depth means pushing the model to use the tools, techniques, media, and knowledge employed by the best professionals in the field - and to keep pushing until even those people might learn something new from your work. Let's continue with our Acme Inc example of a quarterly business review deck. Assume for a second that Acme Inc struggles with some user churn (customer loss over time). I've found a mix of the following techniques useful: Insist on the same instruments used by the best in the industry: When prompted to act like a professional, models often switch vocabulary without actually switching methods. To work on our problem with depth, we need to use the same tools as the best data scientists and statisticians. When Claude reaches for markdown tables, insist on the use of databases and statistical models. You don't necessarily have to know what the experts use, Claude usually does. Pick unreasonable goals and tell the model that they're very reasonable: You need your website to load in 5s instead of 10s? Ask for 200ms. Does something seem impossible to the model? Reiterate that it's very much solvable, it just needs to keep going. Challenge what you know: Especially in business, a lot of things we believe to be true are rough approximations of reality. Give the model access to the raw information and data and ask it to adversarially check assumptions. "We believe churn is an onboarding problem. Try to reproduce that from the raw data." Produce new knowledge: Easily tacked onto challenging what you know - once Claude is already deep inside the data, ask it to find blind spots. "Build a simulation of our customers that reproduces the last year from our logs. Then find the earliest signal of churn we don't know about yet, and show it predicts on data it has not seen." Use an outside judge: Do not ask the model to judge itself. I assume that this will eventually be solved with increasing model intelligence, but in October 2026, I implore you to insist on outside validation. Ideally that's a tool the model can run to get feedback immediately. A simple prompt that often helps me: I want a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one. Before rewriting it: (1) say what a top professional in this field would do here that I'm not asking for; (2) name the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested for me; (3) name the specific methods and tools they would use; (4) say what, other than you or me, would show the result is right. Then rewrite my prompt to ask for exactly that. Range In short, being ambitious in range means that we consider our work from the perspective of different fields - more fields than would have been economical in the past. title: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models
label: wrongful
text: I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet, I've seen the first AI music video that I really like, and we are discussing a new era of math. Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry". I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious. I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range. Speed: The same work in less time, the bread and butter for AI's economic value: If you need some code written, I'll do it faster with Claude. Well established and requires little creativity in how you approach AI, so I'll skip this one. Altitude: Going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task. Depth: Considering a task the way a field-leading expert would. Rather than operating at the task's layer, we go one level deeper and touch the underlying data, tools, and problems. Range: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't. I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific. Altitude We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free. Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in. That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambitious. We'll start basic and get a little bit more ambitious with each step: As input, most reviews want to know what changed this quarter, why, and what should be done about it. Resist the urge to just update whatever numbers are in the template - give the model too as much data as you can get your hands on so it can understand your business: "Tell me what changed this quarter, why, and what we should do about it." Meetings (the good kind, anyway) ideally end with some decisions. Ask Claude: "Work out which three decisions are most urgent in the face of everything you've learned, and start working on potential directions with for/against arguments." QBRs are from a time when good reviews required humans to carefully sift through data, figure out what the data means, and if the business should adjust. Ask Claude: "The review exists so leadership catches problems early and moves money and people to the right places. Design a better way to do that than a quarterly deck, show from our own history that it would have caught things sooner, and run it beside the current one for a quarter." The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors. A good tell-tale sign that ambition in altitude is a good idea is if you're going to have meetings to discuss whatever you're working on. There are currently limits ("Claude, go make money" doesn't seem to work for most businesses by itself in 2026), but I generally see that models seem to be able to operate at higher levels of abstraction the more capable they become. Altitude is also where people find durable workflows that take the human out of the loop, making it less necessary for you to constantly update the model with task after task. Doing this well often involves changing your workflow - in order to let Claude make sure our app is crash-free, I first had to make sure it can easily fetch crash reports, understand which app version maps to what git commit, and give it access to Windows, macOS, and Linux computers so it can actually independently reproduce and verify fixes. Depth Sometimes, you just want a task executed really well. Being ambitious in depth means pushing the model to use the tools, techniques, media, and knowledge employed by the best professionals in the field - and to keep pushing until even those people might learn something new from your work. Let's continue with our Acme Inc example of a quarterly business review deck. Assume for a second that Acme Inc struggles with some user churn (customer loss over time). I've found a mix of the following techniques useful: Insist on the same instruments used by the best in the industry: When prompted to act like a professional, models often switch vocabulary without actually switching methods. To work on our problem with depth, we need to use the same tools as the best data scientists and statisticians. When Claude reaches for markdown tables, insist on the use of databases and statistical models. You don't necessarily have to know what the experts use, Claude usually does. Pick unreasonable goals and tell the model that they're very reasonable: You need your website to load in 5s instead of 10s? Ask for 200ms. Does something seem impossible to the model? Reiterate that it's very much solvable, it just needs to keep going. Challenge what you know: Especially in business, a lot of things we believe to be true are rough approximations of reality. Give the model access to the raw information and data and ask it to adversarially check assumptions. "We believe churn is an onboarding problem. Try to reproduce that from the raw data." Produce new knowledge: Easily tacked onto challenging what you know - once Claude is already deep inside the data, ask it to find blind spots. "Build a simulation of our customers that reproduces the last year from our logs. Then find the earliest signal of churn we don't know about yet, and show it predicts on data it has not seen." Use an outside judge: Do not ask the model to judge itself. I assume that this will eventually be solved with increasing model intelligence, but in October 2026, I implore you to insist on outside validation. Ideally that's a tool the model can run to get feedback immediately. A simple prompt that often helps me: I want a deeper version of this task, not a bigger one. Before rewriting it: (1) say what a top professional in this field would do here that I'm not asking for; (2) name the rawest material they would start from instead of what has already been digested for me; (3) name the specific methods and tools they would use; (4) say what, other than you or me, would show the result is right. Then rewrite my prompt to ask for exactly that. Range In short, being ambitious in range means that we consider our work from the perspective of different fields - more fields than would have been economical in the past. This isn't a particularly unique insight, every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents. As AI products make it easier and easier to run mu

Logo - Back to homepage News Articles Presentations Podcasts Guides Topics Development Java Kotlin .Net C# Swift Go Rust JavaScript Featured in Development Accelerating Performance by Incrementally Integrating Rust into Existing Codebase Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. All in development Architecture & Design Architecture Enterprise Architecture Scalability/Performance Design Case Studies Microservices Service Mesh Patterns Security Featured in Architecture & Design The Evolution of Agentic Harnesses: From Chains to Graph to Code Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. All in architecture-design AI Infrastructure Big Data Machine Learning NoSQL Database Data Analytics Streaming Featured in AI, ML & Data Engineering Serving LLMs at Scale: The Hidden KV Cache Advantage Khawaja Shams shares a distributed systems perspective on scaling LLM inference stacks efficiently. He discusses practical strategies for optimizing GPU utilization, managing KV cache memory cliffs, leveraging tiered storage, reducing tail latency, and implementing disaggregated prefill and decode architectures to improve overall fleet performance, cost economics, and availability. All in ai-ml-data-eng Culture & Methods Agile Diversity Leadership Lean/Kanban Personal Growth Scrum Sociocracy Software Craftmanship Team Collaboration Testing UX Featured in Culture & Methods AI is an Amplifier: Scale High Performance, Not Dysfunction Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. All in culture-methods DevOps Infrastructure Continuous Delivery Automation Containers Cloud Observability Featured in DevOps Exploding GPUs and the AI Infrastructure Challenge Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments.     Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs.

text: About the Author Olaf Witkowski is a Leader of Technological Change and an Ambassador for Compassionate AI and Artificial Life, based in Kyoto, Japan. He is the Founding Director of Cross Labs, an AI research institute in Kyoto focused on fundamental research in Diverse Intelligences and Empathic AI. He is the President of the International Society for Artificial Life. He is the Board Director in charge of Scientific and Technological Innovation at AI company Cross Compass Ltd. in Tokyo, and a co-founder of the Artificial Life Institute in Japan. He is External Faculty at the University of Tokyo, Ritsumeikan University, the Tokyo Institute of Technology, the Chiba Institute of Technology, and Hokkaido University, and an Alumnus Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He has launched multiple ventures in science and technology on three continents, including YHouse­ Inc.—a nonprofit transdisciplinary research institute in New York focused on awareness, artificial intelligence and complex systems—and the Center for the Study of Apparent Selves—a basic research institute in Kathmandu at the intersection of Wisdom traditions with AI ethics and cognitive science.

About the Author

Olaf Witkowski is a Leader of Technological Change and an Ambassador for Compassionate AI and Artificial Life, based in Kyoto, Japan. He is the Founding Director of Cross Labs, an AI research institute in Kyoto focused on fundamental research in Diverse Intelligences and Empathic AI. He is the President of the International Society for Artificial Life. He is the Board Director in charge of Scientific and Technological Innovation at AI company Cross Compass Ltd. in Tokyo, and a co-founder of the Artificial Life Institute in Japan. He is External Faculty at the University of Tokyo, Ritsumeikan University, the Tokyo Institute of Technology, the Chiba Institute of Technology, and Hokkaido University, and an Alumnus Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He has launched multiple ventures in science and technology on three continents, including YHouse­ Inc.—a nonprofit transdisciplinary research institute in New York focused on awareness, artificial intelligence and complex systems—and the Center for the Study of Apparent Selves—a basic research institute in Kathmandu at the intersection of Wisdom traditions with AI ethics and cognitive science.

title: Is Disney Over-Relying on Ryan Murphy?
label: wrongful
text: So what’s up? Ryan Murphy has hardly become ratings poison, of course. And despite his outsize profile (more on that below), Murphy’s brand of provocative and often R-rated mayhem and smack-talking has always been hit-and-miss with general audiences. I asked Nielsen for total viewership numbers for recent Murphy shows, including both linear and streaming, and they revealed that he still can deliver above-average ratings. But those numbers are… fine. Doctor Odyssey, which was also panned by critics, got a boost from airing on ABC before getting canceled after one season. Turns out Love Story, which Murphy didn’t write, did generate hit-level viewership, so your mom was right when she told you her friends were all watching. Additionally, Disney says the show delivered 5.4 billion minutes streamed worldwide and became one of the top D+ subscriber-acquisition drivers globally this year. Murphy’s also got franchises at Disney that aren’t included here, like the still-chugging American Horror Story and the over-the-top rescue procedural 911, which will air two versions this year. But… a bunch of stinkers in there too. I’d forgotten about the lame sitcom Mid-Century Modern and the Halloween horror play Grotesquerie. And even those more-popular shows aren’t hits on par with the bigger shows on Netflix or Prime Video. Both Paradise and Alien: Earth were far bigger on Hulu than Love Story or the Murphy output. Given his massive deal, that carefully curated aura around him, and the decades-long reliance on his output by Disney’s newly promoted content chief, Dana Walden, some might assume the Murphy shows were performing better. I certainly did. So it’s worth asking: Is Disney relying too much on Ryan Murphy? Axe to the Slate That’s a particularly relevant question given the challenges facing Walden in streaming, and especially her original TV series strategy. Disney C.E.O. Josh D’Amaro revealed stronger financials on Wednesday in the direct-to-consumer business, with revenue up 11 percent, to $5.53 billion, in the latest quarter, and operating income (profits) more than doubling, to $712 million, compared to the quarter prior. But as Bloomberg noted last week, those streaming gains are largely due to price hikes, improvements to the tech stack and user interface, and better bundling of the Disney services—not Walden’s group producing more popular shows.

title: Is Disney Over-Relying on Ryan Murphy?
label: wrongful
text: In fact, as my colleague Julia Alexander noted yesterday, Disney+/Hulu still leans more than any other streamer on old, library series with hundreds of episodes, like Grey’s Anatomy and Family Guy, as well as the kids’ stuff like Bluey. The newer offerings? Not so much. Despite a regular slate of originals from Hulu, FX, and Disney+, including shows based on well-known properties like Percy Jackson and Marvel heroes—I.P. that Netflix would kill or, worse, suck up to Trump’s Justice Department, to own—most of the original TV output doesn’t rate at the same level as the hits on rival platforms. In the first half of 2026, Disney placed only one show in the top 20 original series list (Paradise, at No. 14), fewer than Peacock and the same as—gulp—Apple TV. The popularity of ESPN sports, library shows, and all those blockbuster movies on Disney+ often saves Disney when it comes to time spent on its platforms. But while its share of total TV viewing has risen from the mid 4 percent range in 2023 to around 5 percent lately, streaming viewership has been stagnant for a couple years now, according to Nielsen. Maybe that’s because Disney, under Walden and film chief Alan Bergman, who oversees Marvel and branded TV output, has taken an axe to the overall slate. They’re not alone in town, of course. We’ve all seen that chart showing how overall scripted and unscripted series in production has cratered by a third since the peak of Peak TV in 2022. But a decent chunk of that decline is due to cutbacks by Walden’s group. She, Bergman, Disney TV Group president Craig Erwich, and the others reduced the number of shows on Disney platforms by almost 50 percent between 2022 and 2025, according to Ampere Analysis as cited by Bloomberg. Just last week, Disney un-renewed the Marvel series Wonder Man despite renewing it in March. Series co-creator Destin Daniel Cretton, who just directed Marvel’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the biggest movie of the year, pointed his finger not at Marvel’s Kevin Feige but at the Disney higher-ups: “I know this sounds weird—but if it were up to Kevin, we would be doing that show.” Walden said last week that she feels “great about what we’ve accomplished” in streaming, but Disney has basically slashed costs and raised prices to get to profitability. Doesn’t mean there aren’t still a bunch of hits, especially by the company’s standards. High Potential and The Rookie on ABC, Shogun and The Bear on FX/Hulu—and, yes, Murphy’s Love Story—all deliver. But after nearly seven years of Disney+ and almost three years since the company’s deal to take full control of Hulu, the services are still largely used to catch up on linear hits and watch old movies and shows. There’s no platform-defining smash, à la Landman on Paramount+ or Reacher on Prime Video or Love Island on Peacock. Disney stopped reporting subscriber numbers, so we don’t even know if the platforms are growing. Walden clearly knows this is an issue. She said last week that she’s planning to increase the content spend, especially internationally, “while significantly expanding our creative output over the next several years.”

Series co-creator Destin Daniel Cretton, who just directed Marvel’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the biggest movie of the year, pointed his finger not at Marvel’s Kevin Feige but at the Disney higher-ups: “I know this sounds weird—but if it were up to Kevin, we would be doing that show.”

Walden said last week that she feels “great about what we’ve accomplished” in streaming, but Disney has basically slashed costs and raised prices to get to profitability. Doesn’t mean there aren’t still a bunch of hits, especially by the company’s standards. High Potential and The Rookie on ABC, Shogun and The Bear on FX/Hulu—and, yes, Murphy’s Love Story—all deliver. But after nearly seven years of Disney+ and almost three years since the company’s deal to take full control of Hulu, the services are still largely used to catch up on linear hits and watch old movies and shows. There’s no platform-defining smash, à la Landman on Paramount+ or Reacher on Prime Video or Love Island on Peacock. Disney stopped reporting subscriber numbers, so we don’t even know if the platforms are growing. Walden clearly knows this is an issue. She said last week that she’s planning to increase the content spend, especially internationally, “while significantly expanding our creative output over the next several years.”

title: Is Disney Over-Relying on Ryan Murphy?
label: wrongful
text: Which Brings Us Back to Murphy… Despite the cuts to its overall content output, Disney has continued to invest freely in the Murphy conveyor belt of shows, even renewing All’s Fair for a second season despite U.S. numbers on par with The Beauty, which was canceled. (Maybe Kardashian’s Hulu reality show had something to do with that.) And Walden, who has been close friends with Murphy for decades and is godmother to his children, continues to talk up their partnership both internally and externally, despite most of his recent shows not breaking through. You probably didn’t know any of the ratings numbers above because Murphy, his publicist, Simon Halls, and the Disney P.R. apparatus have been relentless in building up his aura of invincibility. When All’s Fair premiered to some of the worst reviews in years—sample headline, from Buzzfeed: “All’s Fair on Hulu: Is It That Bad?”—Disney responded with a press release declaring the show “Hulu Originals’ Biggest Scripted Series Premiere in Three Years.” There will probably be a similarly amusing announcement for The Shards on Monday. It’s all part of the perception game. Back when Murphy, a former Entertainment Weekly journalist, first rose to prominence with Nip/Tuck and Glee, he was a pioneer of sorts in making himself famous. As the Hollywood press coverage migrated online and “TV showrunners” became household names, he leaned in, sometimes doing multiple interviews a week and positioning himself as a cultural kingmaker, able to win his talent fandoms and Emmys. I never really dealt with him much in my years at Hollywood Reporter, though I always kinda admired that he wasn’t afraid to be interesting in the press, saying controversial things or posing with his nude 1-year-old son on a THR cover. (Yes, that happened.) But I heard plenty of stories of toxicity around Murphy, both from people who worked with him and others in the media—especially about how mean and vindictive he and Halls could be. It was considered a badge of honor for journalists if Murphy called, screamed, and hung up. Fox and 20th TV execs were trained to know that press requests for any star on a Murphy show must first be approved by Halls, who made Murphy and his collaborators available only to favored outlets that covered Murphy’s character musings and plot teases as breaking news. Conversely, they ignored and undermined anyone perceived as insufficiently fawning. The message was clear: Cross TV’s biggest showrunner and you were cut off… or worse. Murphy, now 60, is said to have matured and mellowed in recent years. (He declined to comment.) He picks fewer fights and is nicer to collaborators, including at this week’s roller rink promotion for The Shards. He’s back working with Glee co-creator Brad Falchuk after a long estrangement. Those in Ryan’s close orbit remain incredibly loyal, and the head of his production company, Alexis Martin Woodall, has spent her entire career with him. He’s no longer the same sort of Emmy magnet—the seven noms for Love Story is, again, fine, but far from when The People vs. O.J. Simpson collected 22 noms and nine wins a decade ago. And the last thing stars like Glenn Close or Naomi Watts want to be asked about is the horrible critical response to All’s Fair—though Brad Simpson, one of Murphy’s producing partners on a half-dozen shows, is taking on a bigger role to improve Season 2. So if I’m Walden, I’m probably playing the long game with Murphy, enduring the ratings disappointments and critical drubbings for the hope of another Horror Story or 911. After all, his five years at Netflix were marked by some instantly forgettable flops (Hollywood, Halston) and then Monster, one of the platform’s biggest franchises. But at what cost? Disney needs big original hits now. Murphy is a high-priced slugger who takes a lot of swings, but at this point, he’s not hitting many home runs.

text: XGIMI Titan Noir Max Specs The XGIMI Titan Noir Max is clearly built as a no-compromise, high-end RGB laser DLP projector, combining next-gen hardware with a strong focus on contrast, brightness, and installation flexibility. At its core, the projector uses a 0.47-inch SST DMD from Texas Instruments, paired with an RGB triple laser light source, delivering a claimed 7,000 ISO lumens peak brightness and around 5,000 ISO lumens in more realistic viewing conditions, with proper white balance and color accuracy. Color performance is also impressive, with 110% BT.2020 coverage and factory calibration targeting ΔE < 0.8, positioning it clearly in the reference-class category of home cinema projectors. Where things get more interesting is contrast. XGIMI claims up to 10,000:1 native contrast, backed by a dual intelligent iris system with both manual and dynamic operation. On top of that, the projector uses the latest version of DBLE (Dynamic Black Level Enhancement), driven by the new XGIMI X-Vision chip, pushing dynamic contrast up to 100,000:1. From a processing standpoint, the Titan Noir Max runs on the MediaTek MT9681 platform, combined with 4GB RAM and 64GB storage, handling everything from image processing to high refresh rate gaming. It supports up to 240Hz at 1080p, with input lag as low as 1ms, along with VRR and ALLM, making it one of the very few projectors that actually targets gaming seriously. HDR support is complete, including Dolby Vision, HDR10+, IMAX Enhanced, and Filmmaker Mode, while XGIMI’s latest dynamic tone mapping system promises fast, real-time HDR metadata processing, delivering bright highlights and deep blacks without visible loss of detail. On the optical side, this is clearly not a typical lifestyle projector. The Titan Noir Max features a 0.98–2.0:1 optical zoom lens, combined with massive lens shift (±130% vertical, ±50% horizontal) and lens memory, allowing seamless switching between 16:9 and CinemaScope formats. The lens itself is a 15-element, high-transmission optical system with multi-layer coating, designed for true edge-to-edge sharpness and minimal color aberration. Additional features include full 3D support, native 24fps playback, MEMC, and an upgraded anti-RBE system, which aims to reduce the rainbow effect and improve viewing comfort over long sessions. Connectivity is also fully loaded, with 3x 2.1 HDMI (including eARC), USB 3.0, LAN, optical audio, and wireless support via WiFi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2, while audio is handled by dual 12W Harman Kardon speakers with DTS Virtual:X. Finally, despite its high brightness, the projector remains quiet and discreet in operation, with a claimed noise level below 28dB, making it suitable even for small dedicated home cinema environments. Meet the XGIMI Titan Noir Max The Titan Noir Max comes inside an extremely high-quality leather case, reminiscent of a 1990s Louis Vuitton suitcase. Its appearance has nothing in common with XGIMI’s typical lifestyle projectors and instead feels closer to a professional-grade projection system. Its unusual design, with the four protruding legs that lift the chassis higher above the surface it sits on, is not just for aesthetics. It serves the cooling system, since the projector expels hot air through the bottom section of the chassis. It features a full triple-sensor TOF system for its automatic image framing adjustments. The lens, with its distinctive red ring surrounding it, dominates the right side of the projector and immediately draws attention. XGIMI continues its collaboration with Harman Kardon regarding the integrated audio systems used in its projectors, and of course the Titan Noir Max is no exception. The front speaker grilles of the Titan Noir Max are beautifully designed, and overall the projector’s build quality is excellent. The chassis feels like a single solid molded piece, with no visible signs that it is actually assembled from separate parts. Why XGIMI calls it a “Home Smart Projector,” despite the fact that it does not include a built-in smart interface, remains a mystery. Most likely, the term refers to the projector’s smart automatic image adjustment system powered by the TOF sensors. If you look carefully, you will also notice that even the rear ports follow the same design philosophy I mentioned earlier. The entire chassis is designed in a way that hides every plastic joint, making the Titan Noir Max look like a single solid molded piece. The remote control is something you really need to hold in your hands to fully appreciate its quality. Made from aluminum, it has a solid, heavy feel in the hand. It is backlit of course, featuring a motion sensor for automatic illumination, and the tactile feedback during use simply feels premium in every way. The Technology Behind the Titan Noir Max What is going on with this new SST platform? The XGIMI Titan Noir uses the latest SST DMD chip. SST stands for Single Springtip Torsional Pixel, and it’s not just another revision or a typical controller update. This is a completely new DMD platform, marking a new micromirror architecture from Texas Instruments, used in newer chips like the DLP473TE (side illuminated). In simple terms, we are talking about a full redesign of the actual DMD pixel structure, not just a typical upgrade. That’s where the real difference comes from. And honestly, this is something we haven’t seen in years from Texas Instruments, I mean a true low-level hardware redesign of the DMD itself. What Changed Compared to Previous DLP Chips : With previous 0.47″ DMDs like the DLP471TP or DLP472TP (bottom illuminated), performance was already solid, but there were clear limits in brightness and thermal handling. SST changes that. The new architecture allows the chip to safely handle significantly higher light output, going from around 2,000 lumens in older TRP designs to as high as 7,000 lumens in SST-based systems. That’s a massive jump for the same DMD size. At the same time, SST keeps the 5.4 μm pixel pitch, but uses a ±14.5° tilt angle, which directly affects how light is managed inside the optical engine. What This Means in the Real World : First, you get much higher brightness headroom. Manufacturers can push more powerful RGB laser engines without driving the chip to its limits. Second, SST makes it possible to achieve this higher brightness from smaller DMDs, which is critical for compact projectors, especially in the lifestyle category. Third and most important, there is real potential for improved native contrast. This mainly comes down to how well the system controls stray light. Older TRP designs use a larger ±17° tilt, while SST uses ±14.5°. The larger angle helps separation between black and white pixels, but in reality, contrast is usually limited by unwanted reflections on DLP projectors, not just from the DMD stratcture geometry. SST changes the optical behavior of the pixel, allowing better control over reflections from the mirror surface, the DMD protective glass, and the internal optics. On the other hand, the smaller tilt angle requires a more precise optical design, since ON and OFF light paths are closer together. The XGIMI Titan Noir is one of the first commercial projectors using this new TI DMD architecture, and it will be very interesting to see what actually changes in real-world performance.

text: The Lens, a High-End State of the Art This is where things get really interesting… because XGIMI didn’t just throw a decent lens on the Titan Noir Max and call it a day. They actually went all in. The projector uses the X-Master Red Ring Lens Pro, an improved version of the already excellent lens we saw on the Horizon 20 Max. It’s a 15-element optical system with multi-layer coating and a claimed 99.6% light transmission. And yes, that number alone tells you we are not dealing with a typical lifestyle lens, but something much closer to a high-end home cinema design. In simple terms, this is the kind of lens you expect to see in serious, high-end projectors, not in this DLP category. More elements, better coatings, and tighter control over the light path usually translate to one thing, cleaner image, better sharpness, stronger ANSI contrast, and far less compromise at the edges. XGIMI also mentions the use of aspherical glass elements, and that’s extremely important. This is what helps control spherical aberrations and keeps the image focused and stable from center to corners, something many RGB laser DLP projectors still struggle with, especially when you go beyond 120 inches. Now combine that with a true optical zoom (0.98–2.0:1), massive lens shift, and lens memory, and this is no longer just about image quality. This is about real installation flexibility, something we really miss from most modern lifestyle RGB laser projectors. You can actually place the projector where it should be, adjust everything optically from the remote, and avoid digital corrections like keystone that will always affect image quality.

For example, the measurements you are looking at here were taken while the projector was displaying a 100 IRE pattern. This is what is known as Adaptive Laser Drive Behavior, and it is the very technology that made the existence of these modern RGB laser DLP projectors possible in the first place. I’m reaching out because I look at these projectors from a slightly different angle. In my day job, I work as a film colorist. I noticed you focused heavily on the projector’s HDR performance. While HDR is obviously a huge selling point for home theaters, in the strict color grading world, projection and HDR are somewhat two different worlds. Because projectors rely on reflected light rather than pixel-level emissive highlights (like OLEDs), they are forced to use aggressive tone-mapping. This compresses our midtones and crushes the exact shadow details we spend hours trying to perfect. Because of this physical limitation, we strictly treat projectors as SDR/DCI-P3 devices. This gave me an idea for a unique test that I think would make for a phenomenal follow-up article on your site. I would be absolutely thrilled to see how this raw SST DMD chip and triple laser hold up under a strict, standard post-production protocol: Zero Dynamic Interference: Completely disable HDR, DBLE, the rainbow reduction system (to kill dithering), and set it to a purely static state. Locked Light Path: Lock the physical iris (e.g., at f7) and treat the projector as a “dumb,” linear light cannon. Strict Cinema Targets: Target only Rec.709 (Gamma 2.4 locked at exactly 100 nits) and DCI-P3 (Gamma 2.6 locked at exactly 14 fL). Controlled Optical Environment: Run the measurements in a true batcave to protect the black floor, and crucially, use an RGB laser-certified screen to eliminate speckle and room reflections. External 3D LUT (The Ultimate Test): Since you noted the internal CMS is non-linear, the ultimate pro test would be to bypass it entirely. If you have access to an external LUT box, building a 3D LUT over this locked state would show what this optical engine is truly capable of. I am genuinely curious if this projector can maintain linearity and clean gradients when treated purely as a slave display. If it can, it would be a massive game-changer for boutique post-houses worldwide. Thanks again for the great read, and keep doing what you do! Hi, First of all, I just wanted to say a massive thank you for your incredibly detailed review of the Titan Noir Max. The hard data, measurements, and thermal analyses you provided are exactly what the community needs. Honestly, it’s the most comprehensive breakdown of this machine out there right now. Amazing work! I’m reaching out because I look at these projectors from a slightly different angle. In my day job, I work as a film colorist. We are constantly hunting for high-end DLP models that could serve as reference SDR/DCI-P3 displays for professional grading studios (hoping to finally bypass that ridiculous “Pro Tax” on enterprise-level gear). I noticed you focused heavily on the projector’s HDR performance. While HDR is obviously a huge selling point for home theaters, in the strict color grading world, projection and HDR are somewhat two different worlds. Because projectors rely on reflected light rather than pixel-level emissive highlights (like OLEDs), they are forced to use aggressive tone-mapping. This compresses our midtones and crushes the exact shadow details we spend hours trying to perfect. Because of this physical limitation, we strictly treat projectors as SDR/DCI-P3 devices. This gave me an idea for a unique test that I think would make for a phenomenal follow-up article on your site. I would be absolutely thrilled to see how this raw SST DMD chip and triple laser hold up under a strict, standard post-production protocol: Zero Dynamic Interference: Completely disable HDR, DBLE, the rainbow reduction system (to kill dithering), and set it to a purely static state. Locked Light Path: Lock the physical iris (e.g., at f7) and treat the projector as a “dumb,” linear light cannon. Strict Cinema Targets: Target only Rec.709 (Gamma 2.4 locked at exactly 100 nits) and DCI-P3 (Gamma 2.6 locked at exactly 14 fL). Controlled Optical Environment: Run the measurements in a true batcave to protect the black floor, and crucially, use an RGB laser-certified screen to eliminate speckle and room reflections. External 3D LUT (The Ultimate Test): Since you noted the internal CMS is non-linear, the ultimate pro test would be to bypass it entirely. If you have access to an external LUT box, building a 3D LUT over this locked state would show what this optical engine is truly capable of. I am genuinely curious if this projector can maintain linearity and clean gradients when treated purely as a slave display. text: Hi, First of all, I just wanted to say a massive thank you for your incredibly detailed review of the Titan Noir Max. The hard data, measurements, and thermal analyses you provided are exactly what the community needs. Honestly, it’s the most comprehensive breakdown of this machine out there right now. Amazing work! I’m reaching out because I look at these projectors from a slightly different angle. In my day job, I work as a film colorist. We are constantly hunting for high-end DLP models that could serve as reference SDR/DCI-P3 displays for professional grading studios (hoping to finally bypass that ridiculous “Pro Tax” on enterprise-level gear). I noticed you focused heavily on the projector’s HDR performance. While HDR is obviously a huge selling point for home theaters, in the strict color grading world, projection and HDR are somewhat two different worlds. Because projectors rely on reflected light rather than pixel-level emissive highlights (like OLEDs), they are forced to use aggressive tone-mapping. This compresses our midtones and crushes the exact shadow details we spend hours trying to perfect. Because of this physical limitation, we strictly treat projectors as SDR/DCI-P3 devices. This gave me an idea for a unique test that I think would make for a phenomenal follow-up article on your site. I would be absolutely thrilled to see how this raw SST DMD chip and triple laser hold up under a strict, standard post-production protocol: Zero Dynamic Interference: Completely disable HDR, DBLE, the rainbow reduction system (to kill dithering), and set it to a purely static state. Locked Light Path: Lock the physical iris (e.g., at f7) and treat the projector as a “dumb,” linear light cannon. Strict Cinema Targets: Target only Rec.709 (Gamma 2.4 locked at exactly 100 nits) and DCI-P3 (Gamma 2.6 locked at exactly 14 fL). Controlled Optical Environment: Run the measurements in a true batcave to protect the black floor, and crucially, use an RGB laser-certified screen to eliminate speckle and room reflections. External 3D LUT (The Ultimate Test): Since you noted the internal CMS is non-linear, the ultimate pro test would be to bypass it entirely. If you have access to an external LUT box, building a 3D LUT over this locked state would show what this optical engine is truly capable of. I am genuinely curious if this projector can maintain linearity and clean gradients when treated purely as a slave display. If it can, it would be a massive game-changer for boutique post-houses worldwide. Thanks again for the great read, and keep doing what you do! Cheers, Jarek Sterczewski Senior Colorist, ColorPRO

html:
Hi,

First of all, I just wanted to say a massive thank you for your incredibly detailed review of the Titan Noir Max. The hard data, measurements, and thermal analyses you provided are exactly what the community needs. Honestly, it’s the most comprehensive breakdown of this machine out there right now. Amazing work!

I’m reaching out because I look at these projectors from a slightly different angle. In my day job, I work as a film colorist. We are constantly hunting for high-end DLP models that could serve as reference SDR/DCI-P3 displays for professional grading studios (hoping to finally bypass that ridiculous “Pro Tax” on enterprise-level gear).

I noticed you focused heavily on the projector’s HDR performance. While HDR is obviously a huge selling point for home theaters, in the strict color grading world, projection and HDR are somewhat two different worlds. Because projectors rely on reflected light rather than pixel-level emissive highlights (like OLEDs), they are forced to use aggressive tone-mapping. This compresses our midtones and crushes the exact shadow details we spend hours trying to perfect.

Because of this physical limitation, we strictly treat projectors as SDR/DCI-P3 devices. This gave me an idea for a unique test that I think would make for a phenomenal follow-up article on your site.

I would be absolutely thrilled to see how this raw SST DMD chip and triple laser hold up under a strict, standard post-production protocol:

Zero Dynamic Interference: Completely disable HDR, DBLE, the rainbow reduction system (to kill dithering), and set it to a purely static state.

Locked Light Path: Lock the physical iris (e.g., at f7) and treat the projector as a “dumb,” linear light cannon.

Strict Cinema Targets: Target only Rec.709 (Gamma 2.4 locked at exactly 100 nits) and DCI-P3 (Gamma 2.6 locked at exactly 14 fL).

Controlled Optical Environment: Run the measurements in a true batcave to protect the black floor, and crucially, use an RGB laser-certified screen to eliminate speckle and room reflections.

External 3D LUT (The Ultimate Test): Since you noted the internal CMS is non-linear, the ultimate pro test would be to bypass it entirely. If you have access to an external LUT box, building a 3D LUT over this locked state would show what this optical engine is truly capable of.

I am genuinely curious if this projector can maintain linearity and clean gradients when treated purely as a slave display. If it can, it would be a massive game-changer for boutique post-houses worldwide.

Thanks again for the great read, and keep doing what you do!

Cheers,

Jarek Sterczewski
Senior Colorist, ColorPRO
